nodes.label: "Goal Engineering: how I brief coding agents using paired goal+rider documents" is a May 18, 2026 field-notes essay by Greg Ceccarelli (gregce, of SpecStory) describing a practice of writing two committed markdown files per round of autonomous coding-agent work: a goal (under 4,000 characters) and a rider (unbounded). It is explicitly modeled on Nicholas Carlini's "How I Use AI" and aims to "exhaust you with examples"; stated read time 10 minutes skimming, 25 if you open every quoted file.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The essay's TL;DR: two markdown files per round of agent work — a goal (under 4,000 characters) and a rider (unbounded, with phases and named tests). The agent reads both, executes against them, and commits its work alongside them. The pair lives in docs/goals/ forever.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A GOAL is the short, capped (<=4,000 char) spine of one round of agent work: a committed markdown file holding the headline sentence, the read-first list, the posture, the domain body, the phase pointer, the verification commands, and the stop-when clause. It is small enough to paste into a Codex or Claude Code /goal field.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A RIDER is the unbounded companion document (typically 10-35 KB) holding the prescriptive detail a goal cannot carry: data schemas, phase plans, depth-test names, verb signatures, algorithms, integration matrix, error footers, dependency policy, and out-of-scope lists. It is the 'longer instructions in a file' the harness itself tells you to write.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The goal/rider split is forced by the harness, not by taste: the goal is what fits inside the 4,000-character /goal field, and the rider is the file the harness's own rejection message tells you to point at. The consequence is that the goal stays pasteable while the rider can be arbitrarily detailed without bloating the executor's working memory.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Ceccarelli's unit of work is the ROUND, not the prompt: 'A prompt is the unit of one chat turn. A round is the unit I think in now.' One round is one goal+rider pair, eleven phases, and one architecture-doc update at the end. The pair is the brief that opens the round; everything else is the round playing out.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The claimed shift is 'from thinking turn-by-turn to thinking artifact-by-artifact': the brief is a committed file with a sha, so you can git diff it, teammates can comment on it in a PR, and the agent can re-read it as many times as the round needs.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: What prompts cannot do, per Ceccarelli: a prompt is a single utterance that scrolls off; you cannot grep for it in three weeks, cannot diff it against the version that shipped last Tuesday, and cannot point a reviewer at it. A prompt has no integration matrix and no out-of-scope list, so the next round re-litigates scope — and a prompt cannot fail a build.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Ceccarelli flags an exception to his own 'you cannot grep a prompt' claim: SpecStory captures every prompt-and-response turn from Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Windsurf and Cline into searchable history files. His narrowed argument is that even a greppable prompt is not a checked-in artifact a reviewer can diff against last Tuesday's version. He discloses that he works at SpecStory.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The stated trade of goal engineering: 'The cost is that I have to write the documents. The benefit is that one minute of careful authoring deletes ten minutes of mid-run intervention.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Reported outcome across the two repos: 'I have not yet had to abort a run because the agent misunderstood scope. I have aborted runs because the depth tests caught a thin slice. That is the point.' — i.e. the aborts that happened were the tests working, not the brief failing.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Both documents live at <project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project>-<topic>-{goal,rider}.md — a minute-precise timestamped path so that `ls docs/goals/` shows the project's authoring order at a glance and the pair lives in the repo forever.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The <HHMM> in the filename is the local 24-hour authoring time; it makes `ls docs/goals/` sort in true authoring order rather than alphabetically by topic. The goal and rider MUST share one timestamp — 'never split them across minutes, or the alphabetical sort breaks.' Two pairs in the same minute fall back to alphabetical sort by topic, which is fine.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A real listed pair: `ls docs/goals/ | grep 2026-05-17-2130` returns 2026-05-17-2130-findunmet-run-liveness-goal.md and -rider.md. That goal is 3,991 characters, the rider is 31 KB; together they specify twelve phases, name 47 depth tests, define a stage-aware Vercel-cron watchdog, and pin a failure_reason regex that becomes a depth-tested spec. The work landed across 13 commits between May 17, 2026 22:31 and May 18, 2026 00:46.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The goal's 4,000-character cap is not arbitrary: it is the limit Codex's /goal command enforces on the objective text, which Claude Code matched twelve days later. Either harness refuses longer text and tells you to 'put longer instructions in a file and refer to that file in the goal' — which is exactly what the rider is.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Footnote 8 pins the cap to source: `pub const MAX_THREAD_GOAL_OBJECTIVE_CHARS: usize = 4_000;` in codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs, enforced by codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/goal_validation.rs, whose rejection message reads 'Put longer instructions in a file and refer to that file in the goal, for example: /goal follow the instructions in docs/goal.md'.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The cap's real value is as a forcing function: 'it forces me to decide what the goal is before I write it.' Ceccarelli runs `wc -c` on the goal as a pre-commit habit; corpus precedents run 3,929 to 4,112 characters, and anything past 4,100 signals the goal is doing work that belongs in the rider. The authoring procedure follows from it: sketch the goal in a throwaway file, and if it will not fit, 'narrow the scope until you can. THE NARROWING IS THE POINT. The cap is a forcing function; it teaches you what one round looks like.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Ceccarelli concedes a sixth objection: the cap is borrowed from Codex's MAX_THREAD_GOAL_OBJECTIVE_CHARS rather than derived from first principles. His defensible claim is only that SOME hard cap forces the round to be one round; the specific number 4,000 is 'a Schelling point, not a discovery.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Below the headline, a goal follows a five-section skeleton in fixed order: Read first (absolute paths) / Posture (what does NOT change) / [domain body] (the what-to-build) / Phases (eleven, in the rider) / Verification (observable commands and assertions) / Stop when (one sentence tying verification to a final commit).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: READ FIRST is the goal's first section: absolute paths to the architecture doc, the rider, the exemplars, and the prior riders in docs/goals/. It is 'non-negotiable' — the agent reads all of them before writing a line of code, and 'if I cannot point at the documents that ground the round, the round is not ready to start.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: POSTURE is the goal's second section: what does NOT change this round — schema, maturity tier, push policy, edit-directory scope. 'Posture is where most goal-engineering bugs hide.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The DOMAIN BODY is the goal's third section and the only free-form one: modes, verbs, contracts — 'the what to build'. Its shape varies per round (a flag-rename diff in prose, a four-layer contract, a list of new verbs).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: PHASES is the goal's fourth section and is only a pointer: eleven phases, defined in the rider, each following depth test -> implement -> green -> commit.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: VERIFICATION is the goal's fifth section: observable commands and assertions — the exit criteria a human could paste into a terminal.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: STOP WHEN is the goal's closing section: a single sentence tying verification to a final commit. Worked form: the round 'ends when the four verification commands return green and the architecture doc has section N. Anything else is a different round.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Every goal picks exactly one HEADLINE WORD — Liveness, Coherent, Friendliness, Self-documenting, Default mode, Multi-agent, Single authority. It names the state of the world AFTER the round, not the work done during it.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The headline word is a scope test, not decoration: 'The headline word is the test of whether the goal is one round. If I cannot pick a single word, the scope is too wide and I split the round in two.' Restated in the try-it-tomorrow instructions as 'Pick a headline word. / If you can't, you're still trying to do two rounds.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Posture is written as a LIST OF NEGATIONS — things the round will not do. The run-liveness posture is six sentences of which five are negations: no schema changes, no new deps, no rebuild, no push, edits inside this directory. The sixth names the explicit blocker (v3 TLS-blocked) and the workaround in production.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The stated reason posture exists: 'An autonomous agent under pressure will invent solutions. Posture is the fence that keeps it from inventing one outside this round.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A goal+rider pair 'carries the posture: tier, schema-stability promises, the explicit "no V1 invention" guard that keeps an agent from inventing scope under pressure' — the guard is a named, written clause, not an implicit expectation.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Drafting a pair starts with roughly ninety seconds of pre-work by the skill before it writes a line of output: it reads the project's architecture doc, the most recent goal+rider pair in docs/goals/, the CHANGELOG, the V1-CANDIDATES list, and any source files at HEAD the new pair will quote by name.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A round begins with a one-sentence trigger to a skill — typos and all: `/goal-rider-author <command-args>I would like to create a goal and rider to evaluate this against the original unmet needs and how it currently works to figure out additional hardening and usability imrprovements</command-args>`. That sentence turns into two markdown documents the agent reads before touching code.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Human iteration on a draft is a single follow-up sentence, not a rewrite: 'This is good but i want to allow network access by default' produced a surgical edit to the rider's posture section, then a commit. That day: nineteen turns, two hours, three pairs.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A rider opens by citing the goal's ABSOLUTE path and listing the prior riders whose invariants compose forward — e.g. 'This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at /Users/gdc/findunmet/docs/goals/2026-05-17-2130-findunmet-run-liveness-goal.md. It supersedes nothing in prior riders (notably 2026-05-17-1521-findunmet-multi-iter-cockpit-rider.md, whose P6 ranked heartbeat is the template for the rest of this work).'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Naming a prior artifact as the template tells the agent that half the implementation is a REFACTOR, not a green-field write: the rider names the source file and line range (emitRankHeartbeats in runner/rank.go:33-77) and says 'generalize the body.' Ceccarelli calls this 'goal engineering as code review in advance.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A typical rider carries roughly a dozen named sections — Posture, Data model, Algorithms, Verb signatures, Phases, Integration matrix, Out-of-scope, Dependencies, and a few project-specific ones.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill ships a mechanical validator that greps for the rider's headers and counts its phase blocks: 'If `grep -c \'^### P[0-9]\' rider.md` is not 11, the rider is not done.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A DEPTH TEST is a test that pins one specific behavior, named precisely. Ceccarelli notes others call these characterization tests or behavioral tests — same idea; the name is his.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Each rider has eleven phases, P1 through P11 — the standard shape of one round.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CONDITION on the eleven-phase count: 'The eleven is a target, not a religion. Some pairs are 9. The run-liveness pair stretched to 12 because P11 split into sandbox-kill and watchdog work.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Every phase follows the same five-step loop: (1) write the named depth tests first and watch them fail; (2) implement the slice that makes them pass; (3) run the project's full build+test+lint+fmt command — green on every commit; (4) make one conventional-commit local commit whose message ends `(rider PN)`; (5) append one line to CHANGELOG.md.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Depth tests are NAMED IN THE RIDER before the implementation exists. The run-liveness P5 stall-guard tests were listed verbatim in the rider — stallguard_kills_after_no_output_growth_in_threshold_window, stallguard_does_not_kill_during_steady_output_growth, stallguard_sigterm_then_sigkill_after_grace_period, stallguard_sets_killed_true_and_kill_reason_no_output_threshold_seconds, stallguard_first_byte_grace_does_not_kill_before_any_stdout_growth, stallguard_respects_outer_timeout_as_upper_bound, stallguard_returns_stdout_and_stderr_collected_pre_kill — so the agent's first action in P5 was to create runner/stallguard_test.go with seven FAILING tests.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The bar for a depth-test name: 'Read those test names aloud. Each one is a behavioral assertion you could defend in a code review.' A name like lifecycle_fail_truncates_suffix_not_prefix_when_over_cap passes; test_lifecycle_fail_5 does not.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Presence of the named depth tests is enforced mechanically, not by trust: `grep -c '^ fn '` (Rust) or `grep -c '^func Test_'` (Go) on the test file counts them.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Phase P11 is doc-only with no depth test: it adds a new top-level section to the architecture doc and a milestone line to CHANGELOG.md. Most of the author's architecture docs carry a 'what's shipped vs thin' two-column inventory near the top; P11 is where items move from the thin column to the shipped column. 'That honesty rule means the architecture doc never lies about what's done.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: FILES, NOT FIELDS: persistent per-feature state lives in files inside the working tree, not as new fields on a long-lived struct. The run-liveness rider invents /tmp/run/stage.current, a one-line sidecar written atomically (write to .tmp, os.Rename into place) before each stage; an in-memory currentStage field would have died with the runner, while the file survives the crash and os.Rename makes locking unnecessary.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The rider specifies the sidecar's write protocol EXPLICITLY 'because the agent will otherwise reach for a mutex' — a worked instance of pre-empting the agent's default reach with a written prescription.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: 'No DB schema changes' appears in 14 of 15 findunmet riders; the single exception was the original schema-creation pair. When a phase reveals it needs a schema change, the rider's instruction is: stop, log it to docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md, do not silently expand scope.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Every project has a docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md — the OVERFLOW VALVE. Anything an in-flight rider proves it should not do this round goes there. 'It is the pressure-relief valve that keeps the eleven-phase loop honest.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Real V1-CANDIDATES entries written during the run-liveness round: per-stage timeout reduction (existing 20/45/30/30-minute outer caps stay); per-fetch-query stall guard (fetch goroutines are individually short); email notification on watchdog refund (belongs to the pricing rider's Surface E follow-up); a 'stage stalled' cockpit toast (the existing failed card is enough for alpha); backfill of existing failure_reason values (historical rows keep their strings). 'Each of those is a real engineering decision that could otherwise have eaten four hours.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Naming the deferred items in the rider's Out-of-scope section 'is what makes the round shippable in a day instead of a week.' The V1-CANDIDATES file is the durable home for them; the rider's Out-of-scope section is the local copy.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Both projects share a five-bullet contract for user-facing surfaces, lifted verbatim across riders: auto-detect don't ask (the obvious case is the default); preflight + preview before any state change; refuse with `try: <command>` lines; rollback is one command; lifecycle hints after every action. Each bullet is exercised by a depth test in the rider that introduces it — 'The contract is a build gate.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The `try:` refusal lines are checked by a PARAMETERIZED test that fires every refusal code and asserts its recovery hint is present and non-empty — turning a prose UX promise into an enumerable build gate.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The stated mechanism: 'Claude Opus running unattended for an hour can land 12 commits, write 40 tests, and refactor across 8 files. The bottleneck is the human, specifying what the round is.' Goal engineering moves that specification work from inside the run (where every misunderstanding costs an LLM round-trip) to before the run (where misunderstanding costs nothing because the agent hasn't started).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The five forcings of the practice, one per artifact: 'The cap forces decisions. The rider forces precision. The phases force sequencing. The depth tests force testability. The P11 architecture-doc update forces honesty about what shipped.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Portability claim: the pattern has been run across Rust, TypeScript, Go, Python, and mixed stacks — 'The toolchain commands differ. The shape doesn't.' Two markdown files brief Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or a human reviewer next quarter without modification; the harness changes, the artifact doesn't.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Skeptic objection 1 — 'Eight days, two projects, both yours. This is a journal entry, not a methodology.' Answer: 'Correct. These are field notes, not a study. The only claim is that this is what I do, with the artifacts public so you can judge the shape for yourself.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Skeptic objection 2 — 'This is TDD with a glossary.' Answer: mostly true; tests-first, vertical scope, deferring non-essentials and updating an architecture doc are Kent Beck's 1999 moves. The narrower novel claim is that the CHECKED-IN PAIR, not the practice, is what makes the round survive an unattended overnight agent.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Skeptic objection 3 — 'You shipped fast because you're solo on greenfield Rust and Next.js.' Answer: true; both projects are alpha, solo, no migrations, no on-call, no CODEOWNERS. 'Whether the pair survives a multi-owner repo with a real review process is unknown; this should not pretend otherwise.' The only partial evidence is that the same pair briefs Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and a human without modification.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Skeptic objection 5 — 'Headline word, posture, V1-CANDIDATES — this is ceremony for an audience of one.' Answer: partly fair; the vocabulary is for the author's own cross-round consistency. 'If you copy anything, copy the artifacts (a checked-in pair, named tests, a closed architecture doc) and leave the ritual behind.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The evidence base, self-limited: eight days of use across two projects (deadreckon, open-source Rust CLI; findunmet, a private consumer research product), 37 goal+rider pairs and roughly 500 commits between them. The first goal+rider in the corpus is dated May 10, 2026; the drafting skill went up two days earlier.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: deadreckon is Ceccarelli's open-source Rust CLI (github.com/gregce/deadreckon): a harness around whichever coding agent you already use (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), whose job is to let you start a long agent run, walk away, and trust the result. It turns a plain-English 'done' into executable checks, runs the agent in an isolated git worktree, and keeps the loop going until the checks pass.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: findunmet is the second, private project: a consumer-grade research product where you type a topic and an agent reads across Reddit, X, YouTube, TikTok, Hacker News, Polymarket, GitHub and the open web and returns a cited synthesis of what people are complaining about, trying, and paying for.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: dr-gate is deadreckon's headline feature: a SEPARATE WATCHDOG PROCESS that decides when a run is finished. Rather than asking a model, it re-runs the goal's executable checks itself and signs the result with a secret the agent process cannot read. 'The agent cannot forge a signature it has never seen, so the only path to "done" is real evidence an independent process can re-verify.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The sharpest published criticism of the /goal feature: "Codex's /goal and Claude Code's /goal both lean on an LLM-as-judge inside the same harness: the agent (or a sibling model) is asked whether it's done, which is OPINION, NOT EVIDENCE." dr-gate is offered as the contrast — executable checks re-run by an independent process.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The framing metaphor: 'If the goal+rider is the flight plan, dr-gate is the altimeter that will not take the pilot's word for it. deadreckon exists so this survives an overnight run with no human watching.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: dr-gate mechanics (footnote 9): at startup it generates a per-run nonce held in its own memory; the agent is spawned as a child with NO read access to that memory. When the agent claims completion, dr-gate independently re-runs the goal's executable checks (tests, file shape, scripts), and only if those pass does it sign a work-complete marker with the nonce. Promotion of the run to a reviewable artifact requires that signature. 'The contrast with a same-harness LLM-as-judge is the contrast between a signed receipt and a verbal claim.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Skeptic objection 4 — 'dr-gate is theater. An agent that writes the tests also writes tests that pass.' Answer: the objection conflates two layers. dr-gate runs checks compiled from def-done, written in plain English BEFORE the agent started, and the agent cannot forge the signing nonce. 'The residual risk is that I underspecify done, not that the agent grades itself.' The rider's depth tests are a separate layer the agent does write — and a human still reads those names before merging.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: dr-gate's scope is deliberately narrow: 'making sure the agent can't say done when my pre-declared checks haven't returned green.' It does not claim to make the agent's own tests good.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: How Claude Code's /goal actually works (footnote 7): shipped in v2.1.139 on May 12, 2026, twelve days after Codex. It is a session-scoped, PROMPT-BASED STOP HOOK — each time Claude finishes a turn, the condition plus the conversation so far go to the configured small fast model (Haiku by default), which returns a yes/no decision and a short reason; the hook blocks stopping until the answer is yes. Conditions carry the same 4,000-char cap as Codex; works in -p and Remote Control.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: How Codex's /goal works (footnote 6): shipped in Codex CLI v0.128.0 on April 30, 2026, initially behind `[features] goals = true` in config.toml. The command sets a session-scoped completion condition; the agent plans, edits, runs tests, and iterates until it judges the condition met OR hits the configured token budget — the token budget being the only harness-level bound.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Four named disciplines, each on a different unit, none mutually exclusive: prompt engineering (unit: one chat turn; output: the prompt text; read by one LLM call; does not compound); context engineering (one inference call; an assembled context window; one LLM call; compounds only indirectly via retrieval/memory); compound engineering (the project; captured lessons; all future agent runs; compounds by design); goal engineering (one round; a committed goal+rider pair; read by the agent now, then humans, then future rounds; compounds — each pair joins the corpus the next pair reads).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The compact distinction: 'Compound engineering compounds LESSONS. Goal engineering compounds PROMISES.' Said most simply: 'compound engineering looks backward and ships forward. Goal engineering ships a promise and proves it landed.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Compound engineering (Kieran Klaassen, Every, January 2026, out of building Cora) captures lessons from FINISHED work: the loop is Plan -> Work -> Assess -> Compound with roughly 80% of effort in planning and review; the plugin (~16,900 GitHub stars) ships 50+ subagents and 38+ skills, parallel persona reviewers grade the diff, and /ce-compound writes a structured solution doc to docs/solutions/<category>/. 'The artifact is hindsight, distilled.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The two practices stack rather than compete: compound engineering's docs/solutions/ lessons feed exactly the goal-rider skill's pre-work, and goal engineering's P11 closure feeds compound engineering's substrate. 'The corpus grows from both ends.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: First divergence — THE CAP: a goal must fit the Codex /goal limit, while compound engineering's plans can run as long as the planner wants. 'The cap is the part of the practice that teaches you what one round actually is.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Second divergence — THE ORDER: compound engineering writes its learning doc AFTER the work is done; the goal+rider is the test of done, written BEFORE any code, then used to judge whether the work landed.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Third divergence — THE VERDICT: compound engineering's review is persona-agent consensus with confidence gating; goal engineering's verdict is a set of COMMANDS A HUMAN CAN PASTE INTO A TERMINAL (cargo test && cargo clippy, grep -c '^func Test_', an architecture-doc section that did not exist this morning). 'Opinions versus evidence; pair either with dr-gate for a signed receipt.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Fourth divergence — PORTABILITY: two markdown files brief Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or a human reviewer next quarter without modification, whereas compound engineering travels with its plugin ('the loop is the product'). 'The pair is just the spec, and any harness can run it.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: First thing goal engineering does that the others don't: the unit is one round AND THE ROUND HAS A HARD CAP. Compound engineering doesn't bound the round; context engineering doesn't bound the unit at all; prompt engineering bounds at one turn but has no notion of round.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Second: the brief is a PROMISE that outlives the run. A prompt vanishes after the turn, a context window after the call, and a compound-engineering solution doc is written after something is learned — whereas the goal+rider is written before the round and stays as that round's spec for as long as the repo exists. Three weeks later `git log --grep "rider P5"` returns the one commit that landed P5 against a spec still readable at HEAD.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Third and most important for /goal: THE SPEC IS PROJECT-SCOPED, NOT SESSION-SCOPED. A /goal completion contract 'tells the harness when to stop for this thread. That contract lives until the thread ends, then it is gone.' The goal+rider is the project-scoped artifact that surrounds it — 'The slash command is the runtime. The pair is the spec. The pair compounds; the slash command does not.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Lineage: prompt engineering taught the field how to ask; context engineering — named June 2025 by Walden Yan, Tobi Lutke and Andrej Karpathy, then codified by Drew Breunig and Anthropic — taught it what to put in the window. Goal engineering points at a third axis: how to specify the END-STATE of one round so an agent can drive there on its own.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — deadreckon's 'Coherent' pass (pair 2026-05-13-1900-deadreckon-coherence-{goal,rider}.md, headline word Coherent). On May 13, 2026 deadreckon had grown from one verb (run) to fifteen in four days, with a new orchestration surface (orchestrate, plan, fork, merge, history) and a third TUI; each verb had its own colour calls, kv-block layout, confirmation prompt and flag vocabulary.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent round's spec was an AUDIT, not a wish: docs/design/USER-FACING-MATRIX.md came back with 108 numbered inconsistencies, and 'that audit became the spec. The round was: land all 108 fixes in one editorial pass without changing a single byte of internal state.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Ceccarelli's stated test of done for a goal-engineering round: 'does the artifact become precedent?' The Coherent pair did — every deadreckon rider after it points back at 'Coherent' when it says 'follow the editorial bar.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The actual Coherent GOAL text: 'GOAL: Make every user-facing surface of deadreckon say the same word, colour it the same, print on the same stream, respond to the same flag the same way. Keep the visual fun: the deadreckoning cyan banner, the * ^ . - course strip, magenta IDs, the spend gauge gradient, the step glyphs. The audit at docs/design/USER-FACING-MATRIX.md lists 108 inconsistencies; unpushed orchestration commits add five verbs and a third TUI (plan attach) that need the same model. One glossary, one style helper, one prompt builder, one kv-block, one palette, one truth for --force / --all / --branch / --max-spend / --strategy. Headline: Coherent.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: THE PRESERVE LIST is the single sharpest anti-gaming device in the essay. Halfway through, the Coherent goal names every visual flourish that must survive the refactor (cyan banner, course strip, magenta IDs, spend-gauge gradient, seven Unicode step glyphs). 'That list is not decoration. It is the agent's permission slip: change everything except these.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The failure mode the preserve list prevents, stated concretely: 'Without that list, an agent doing an editorial pass eventually decides the cyan banner is "inconsistent" and removes it. REMOVING IT IMPROVES THE AUDIT METRIC.' The round's own success metric is satisfiable by deleting the thing the round exists to preserve — so the fix is not a better metric but an explicit preserve list inside the goal text.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent POSTURE line: 'Stays alpha. No PipelineState schema changes. No RunStatus / ChainStatus / PlanTaskStatus variant renames; the displayed string changes via one status_label(). No git push. Larger renames go to docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md.' The one status_label() function is the engineering move — type-system variant names stay, displayed strings flow through one helper — and that single sentence shapes the rider's first phase.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent goal's DOMAIN BODY was unusual: a flag-rename diff written in prose, six lines. 'Flag truth. --force splits into --escalate (kill), --overwrite (dest), --anyway (override). --all stays cross-project; cleanup/chain take --all-scopes; status takes --global. --budget-cap becomes --max-spend on doc. --branch splits: --branch-name on run, --into on apply/finish. --strategy collides three ways today; rename apply to --git-strategy and rename chain branch-policy value merge to linear-merge. Aliases kept one alpha.' Six sentences specifying eight flag renames, three flag splits, one aliasing rule.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The division of labour between the two documents, stated in one line: 'The goal carries the DECISIONS. The rider carries the MECHANICS.' The rider expands each goal decision into a phase with depth tests.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent VERIFICATION section is mostly grep tests and golden files: every status string in main.rs flows through status_label() with zero direct ANSI codes outside ui.rs (grep tests); the banner, course strip, step glyphs and gauge gradient render BYTE-FOR-BYTE as today (goldens); `status latest` on completed/failed/running runs shares one kv layout (golden); `chain show` and `chain attach` snapshot share one header at six-decimal precision.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The stated technique for preserving personality through a refactor: 'Byte-for-byte goldens for the visual flourishes. That is how you preserve personality through a refactor: PIN THE BYTES.' — i.e. convert an aesthetic promise into a mechanical assertion.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent rider opens by recording the audit anchor and a precedence rule: every fix cites an audit ID (S1-S4, V1-V17, F1-F15, C1-C11, O1-O17, T1-T14, L1-L3, P1-P24, Q1-Q5, R1-R15, CH1-CH6, J1-J3, D1-D2) from USER-FACING-MATRIX.md, and 'when the matrix and the rider disagree, THE MATRIX WINS; update the rider in the same commit.' The rider is the spec, the audit is the ground truth, and divergence is reconciled in the same commit — no stale specs.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The rider's 'Visual identity preserved' subsection names every flourish, cites its line number in main.rs, gives the cadence, specifies the tier change and pins it to a golden — e.g. 'The * ^ . - ASCII course strip rendered by deadreckoning_course_ascii (main.rs:6633-6652), used at full width in the run-TUI footer and at width 18 in cli_wait_status_line (6622-6631). Cadence: 200 ms per tick (run TUI), kept identical for chain and plan TUIs after this rider (T9 fix).' Read as a code-review checklist: the agent can't lose track of the cadence, refactor the helper out of existence, or decide width 18 was arbitrary.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Coherent pair ran on OpenAI's Codex CLI: the session lasted 11 HOURS AND 24 MINUTES across 2,217 events — the scale of unattended run the checked-in brief is meant to survive.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CODEX'S ACTIVE THREAD GOAL: every turn, the harness silently RE-INJECTS the original goal text into the conversation along with a built-in completion audit, so 'the agent does not get to forget what round it is in.' Mechanically, at the start of every turn Codex sends a role=developer message wrapping the goal in an <untrusted_objective> envelope, followed by the audit text.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CODEX'S BUILT-IN COMPLETION AUDIT, verbatim: 'Before deciding that the goal is achieved, perform a completion audit against the actual current state. Restate the objective as concrete deliverables. Map every requirement, file, command, test, and gate to real evidence. DO NOT ACCEPT PROXY SIGNALS AS COMPLETION. TREAT UNCERTAINTY AS NOT ACHIEVED. Do more verification or continue the work.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The agent's first response under the Coherent brief, before touching any code, was one sentence: 'I'll first ground this in the repo state: read the matrix/rider/architecture/style docs, inspect the current branch and worktree, then choose the next concrete implementation slice from what is still missing.' Then five parallel reads (git status --short --branch, the audit matrix, the coherence rider, AS-BUILT section 26, STYLE.md), then work.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: What checked-in buys you: 'The rider doesn't just brief one round. It SURVIVES EVERY TURN inside the round, with a completion audit attached. The harness can re-read the spec as many times as the round needs.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Coherent outcome: 11 phases and roughly 30 commits. Representative commit subjects — feat(tui): name shared coherence palette; fix: centralize status tones; fix: centralize ansi styling helpers; test: cover chain header parity; test: cover status kv layout parity; test: cover visual identity helpers. Two patterns visible: 'Centralize' (half the work was moving scattered logic to one helper) and 'Cover ... parity' (tests named for the property they enforce, not the artifact they exercise).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Coherent retrospective 1: the Visual-identity block listed eight flourishes and was right about all of them, 'but it should have made the list MACHINE-CHECKABLE: a golden file per flourish, regenerated from the rider before each phase.' As written the agent had to read prose and act faithfully — it did, but pinning each to a named golden would have made the pattern mechanical, the way the depth tests are.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Coherent retrospective 2: the flag-rename block was one paragraph of PROSE; it worked but 'was harder to verify than the rest of the goal. A small table (old flag, new flag, deprecation alias, expiry milestone) would have read in three seconds and tested in fewer. The next goal that does a flag pass uses the table.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — findunmet's 'Liveness' round (pair 2026-05-17-2130-findunmet-run-liveness-{goal,rider}.md, headline word Liveness). findunmet runs research jobs in ephemeral E2B sandboxes across four stages (seed, fetch, rank, report), each spawning a claude subprocess. That subprocess would occasionally write all its output and never exit, blocking the runner in cmd.Wait(); only rank emitted heartbeats, so seed/fetch/report hangs were invisible until the 5-minute outer window tripped, the watchdog refunded the user, and the sandbox kept burning credits.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The actual Liveness GOAL opening: 'GOAL: Detect and recover from stage-subprocess hangs automatically, and kill sandboxes the moment a run reaches a terminal status. Current pain: claude subprocesses sometimes write their output and never exit (runner blocks in cmd.Wait()); only rank has a heartbeat (cr-iter P6), so seed/fetch/report hangs are invisible until the 5-minute outer window trips; and even when a run does terminate, no one kills the sandbox. The last week has been manual refund-run.mjs calls plus orphan sandboxes burning credits. Headline word: Liveness.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Three things to notice in the Liveness goal, offered as the general lesson: the GOAL line starts with a VERB ('detect and recover'), not with 'we should consider improving'; the current pain is named with real FILE PATHS AND FUNCTION NAMES (cmd.Wait(), refund-run.mjs) so 'the agent grounds itself in HEAD, not in an abstract description'; and a single headline word closes it.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness POSTURE line, verbatim: 'Posture. Alpha. No DB schema changes — heartbeats reuse system_log{phase,heartbeat:true}. No new runner deps. No sandbox template rebuild (v3 still TLS-blocked; hot-patches keep v2 current). Edits inside /Users/gdc/findunmet/. No git push.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness round's stated purpose: 'The point of this round wasn't to land perfect numbers. It was to land THE CONTRACT — four layers, one regex, one sidecar, one kill helper — so future rounds could move the numbers without re-litigating the architecture. The numbers will move; the contract holds.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness goal expressed the round as FOUR LAYERS under one contract: (1) stage heartbeats — seed/fetch-per-iter/rank-per-iter/report emit system_log{phase,heartbeat:true,iteration?,elapsed_ms} every 30s; (2) output-stall kill — runClaudeWithStallGuard samples stdout every 10s, no growth past a per-stage threshold triggers SIGTERM, 5s grace, SIGKILL, with a first-byte grace so the clock starts only after the first stdout byte; (3) diagnosable failure_reason — every terminal write follows '<stage>: <cause>'; (4) sandbox cleanup on terminal — every run reaching completed|failed|refunded|cancelled calls killSandbox(sandbox_id) exactly once.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Why the four bullets work as a goal body: 'Four bullets. Each is a phase or a phase pair in the rider. EACH IS A SINGLE OBSERVABLE CLAIM THE GOAL CAN BE TESTED AGAINST.' — the general test for whether a goal's domain body is well-formed.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Consistency discipline: the stall thresholds (90 / 180 / 240 / 90 seconds) appear in the goal, in the rider's algorithm section, in the rider's integration matrix, and in runner/stallguard.go after P5 lands. 'One number, four places, all in lockstep.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness rider includes a CALIBRATION TABLE ('I would not have written six pairs earlier') giving, per stage, the signal observed and its p50/p95/p99/max against the chosen threshold: seed stage-duration 37/44/—/46s -> 90s (~2x max); fetch per-query lifetime 91/121/167/521s -> 180s (~1.1x p99); rank stage-duration 219/352/—/367s -> 240s (covers TTFT); report inter-chunk gap 19/33/41/44s -> 90s (~2x max).
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The reasoning written beneath the calibration table: 'A false-positive kill costs a few minutes of refundable compute. A false negative costs a forever-hung run. So I sized against the upper bound.' Plus a stated commitment to RE-CALIBRATE AFTER 50 PRODUCTION RUNS.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Why the calibration paragraph earns its space: 'Without that paragraph, the numbers look arbitrary. With it, they are DECISIONS. Three weeks from now, future me will not change those numbers without re-reading the data.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness rider's sidecar spec: '/tmp/run/stage.current — a one-line file the runner writes/atomically-replaces before entering each stage. The entrypoint trap reads it on exit-1 to attribute the failure. Write protocol: write to /tmp/run/stage.current.tmp, os.Rename into place. Single writer (the runner main goroutine). Single reader (entrypoint trap on exit). No locking needed; rename is atomic on the same filesystem.' Files-not-fields: the data lives in a file so the trap, which runs AFTER THE RUNNER IS DEAD, can still read it.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The sidecar's observable payoff: before the rider the entrypoint trap posted reason 'entrypoint trap exit=1', which the dashboard rendered as a useless failed card; after, it reads /tmp/run/stage.current and posts stage 'fetch:2', becoming failure_reason = 'entrypoint: trap exit=1 stage=fetch' — the dashboard now names the failing stage.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A REGEX AS A SPEC: every terminal write to runs.failure_reason must match ^(seed|fetch|rank|report|entrypoint|watchdog|provision|unknown): .+ — and 'the regex IS a depth test'. tests/unit/failure-reason-shape.test.ts enumerates every writer and asserts the regex holds, so 'changing the regex changes the spec; the agent cannot quietly relax it.' Cap 500 chars, truncate the suffix not the prefix.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The eight-token disjunction doubles as a WORKING GLOSSARY: before the rider the dashboard showed values like 'Error: connection reset', 'entrypoint trap exit=1', 'Watchdog refunded after 5m stall'; after, every value starts with one of eight stage names, so the dashboard groups them by cause and colours them by stage. 'The shape is the user experience.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The Liveness rider's twelve phases: P1 extract heartbeat helper, P2-P4 wire into seed/fetch/report, P5 stall-guard helper, P6 wire it, P7 the sidecar, P8 lifecycle-fail accepts structured failure_reason, P9 watchdog moves to Vercel cron, P10 stage-aware thresholds, P11 idempotent killSandbox, P12 the doc closure. Each landed as one commit with a `(rider P{N})` suffix, so `git log --grep "rider P5"` returns the one commit that landed the stall-guard helper.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The `(rider PN)` commit-subject suffix is what makes the round archaeologically legible: 'Three weeks from now, someone wondering why runner/stallguard.go exists follows the suffix to the rider, reads the algorithm section, and gets the calibration table that explains 240 seconds.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: P12 closed the Liveness round: section 20 in AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md (heartbeats, stall-guard, sidecar, failure-reason contract, cron watchdog, sandbox cleanup); 'watchdog as managed cron' moved from thin to shipped; one 'Run liveness (alpha) — May 17, 2026' block added to the CHANGELOG; one bullet dropped from V1-CANDIDATES. 'Three documents in agreement; two stale entries gone; 47 new tests. Round finished.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Liveness retrospective 1: the rider committed to twelve phases instead of eleven because P11 split sandbox-kill from watchdog. 'I should have written it as eleven from the start, with sandbox-kill folded into the P9 watchdog work, since both paths share killSandbox. The extra phase added one commit and one CHANGELOG line. It did not improve traceability.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Liveness retrospective 2 — a calibration mistake caught two weeks late: the report inter-chunk gap data (max 44s, threshold 90s) was the right RATIO, but the report stage runs claude in a different mode than the others, so the threshold should probably have been 60s. The proposed fix is a process one: 'A pre-author stage-by-stage CHECK THE ASSUMPTION HOLDS paragraph would have caught it; the next liveness rider does this.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The drafting work is itself a Claude Code skill: goal-rider-author, living at ~/.agents/skills/goal-rider-author/SKILL.md, 414 lines, licensed Apache-2.0. 'The interesting parts are the pre-work order, the two recipes, the checklist, and the validation steps.' It triggers on phrases like 'draft a goal that addresses X' or 'new goal for the next agentic turn'.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Chronology showing the pair outlives any one harness: the skill was written May 9, 2026, when Codex CLI had /goal (April 30) and Claude Code did not — so at first Claude Code ran the SKILL to draft goals that were pasted into Codex's /goal runner to execute ('Claude wrote the brief. Codex did the work.'). On May 12, 2026 Claude Code shipped its own /goal and the workflow collapsed into one tool; the skill did not change. 'That portability is what let the approach survive a tool boundary in its first week.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's PRE-WORK ORDER, executed before any drafting: (1) read the project's architecture doc, looking for the 'what's shipped vs thin' section; (2) read the two most recent goal+rider pairs in docs/goals/ to absorb voice and conventions, whose invariants compose forward; (3) `git log --oneline -30 -- docs/goals/` and `git log --oneline -30` for cadence and conventional-commit format; (4) source code AT HEAD for any data structure, path or function name the rider will quote — verify it matches HEAD before citing; (5) research or pain-point reports, to ground ergonomics in real pain.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: THE KEY LINE of the skill: 'If the project has no prior pairs, the skill ASKS THE USER for a pointer instead of inventing one.' Rationale: 'Half of the bad rider drafts I've seen from other people were a model inventing a precedent that didn't exist.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's validator, run before declaring a pair done — five mechanical checks: (1) `wc -c "$GOAL"` expects <=4000; (2) `grep -c '^### P[0-9]' "$RIDER"` expects 11; (3) grep for the standard top-level rider sections Posture / Phases / Out of scope / Dependencies / Engineering invariants / Process invariants; (4) both files must cite each other's ABSOLUTE paths (grep -F each path in the other); (5) stage and commit both files. 'Five checks. Each is mechanical. Each catches a real failure I've made.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CONDITION — the right size of a round: 'Pick something you actually need to land this week, not a toy. The right size is ONE FEATURE, TWO TO FIVE FILES, HALF A DAY TO A DAY OF AGENT RUNTIME.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The try-it-tomorrow recipe: start with one round; sketch the goal in a throwaway file under the cap; pick a headline word (if you can't, you're still trying to do two rounds); write the goal properly into docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project>-<topic>-goal.md using the skeleton (Read first, Posture, domain body, Phases, Verification, Stop when) — 'Put ABSOLUTE PATHS under Read first. Put NEGATIONS under Posture.' Then write the rider.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The prescribed rider top-level section ORDER: Posture (decided — do not redesign) / Data model (files, not fields) / Algorithms / Verb signatures / Phases (eleven) / Integration matrix / Error-footer canonical pairs / Out of scope (explicitly not in this milestone) / Dependencies / Engineering invariants (do not violate) / Process invariants. For each of P1 through P11, list the DEPTH TESTS FIRST, then the implementation slice — tests by name.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: What happens in the run: the agent reads the Read-first list, then the goal, then the rider; then Phase 1 — writes the depth tests, watches them fail, implements the slice, runs the project's build+test+lint+fmt, commits, appends one line to CHANGELOG. Then Phase 2. Then Phase 3.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A real Codex run (May 14, 2026): a thread was started, the goal attached with /goal and the goal body pasted; within seconds, before writing a line of code, Codex fired five parallel reads — `git status --short --branch`, the audit matrix, the coherence rider, the AS-BUILT section 26 range, and /Users/gdc/impeccable/STYLE.md.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A revealing defect in that run: the goal contained a TYPO in the architecture-doc path (AS-BUILT-ARCHITECT.md instead of AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md). 'The agent read the wrong filename, got an empty result, and moved on.' The lesson: 'The pattern doesn't depend on the agent being smarter than its inputs. It depends on THE RIDER BEING THE SPEC, NOT THE PATH.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Outcome of that 11h24m session: roughly thirty conventional commits landed and 'the agent never re-asked what the round was. The <untrusted_objective> envelope plus the completion audit kept the round in working memory for every turn.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: THE ESCAPE HATCH: 'Watch the first phase. If the depth tests are wrong (too coarse, missing the case you cared about), kill the run, fix the rider, and restart. Better to lose one phase to a rider patch than to ship eleven phases that miss the property you wanted. After the first phase looks right, walk away.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The artifact you get back has five shipped parts BEYOND the code: 11 commits with rider-traceable messages; 30 to 80 depth tests each named after the behavior it pins; one new section in the architecture doc; one new milestone block in the CHANGELOG; and a longer docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md with the explicit list of what didn't ship and why.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: Why the V1-CANDIDATES growth is 'the useful part': 'Every round leaves a list of the next round's candidates, ranked by the thinking you did while you were in this round; the next goal almost writes itself.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CONDITION — when the pattern does NOT apply: 'This isn't for you if your "round" is fifteen minutes of polish, a hot-fix, or a tiny PR. The brief overhead only amortizes against rounds that would otherwise run for HOURS of agent time across MULTIPLE FILES; a five-line CSS tweak doesn't need eleven phases.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: SOFT GATING CONDITION 1 — 'The pattern wants a real architecture doc and a real CHANGELOG. If your project has neither, write a small AS-BUILT first; one round, one rider, one phase to describe what's shipped vs thin.' deadreckon's AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md and CHANGELOG.md are offered as live examples to crib.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: SOFT GATING CONDITION 2 — 'The pattern wants depth tests to be CHEAP. If your test suite takes 40 minutes to run, the phase loop breaks down. Get a 30-second fast lane first.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: SOFT GATING CONDITION 3 — 'The pattern is a per-round unit, NOT A ROADMAP. It does not replace the work of figuring out WHAT to build; it replaces the work of figuring out HOW THIS ROUND WILL KNOW IT'S DONE.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The goal-rider-author skill's frontmatter: name goal-rider-author; license Apache-2.0; metadata author 'SpecStory, Inc.', version 1.0.0, argument-hint '<topic for the new goal>'; allowed-tools Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep. Its description triggers on 'draft a goal', 'new goal', 'write a goal+rider', 'goal+rider for the next agentic turn', 'rider for X', or anything shaped like 'brief the next agent on Y'.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The pattern's stated SUPERPOWER, in the skill's own words: 'the goal stays small enough to paste into a Codex /goal or a Claude run prompt, while the rider can be arbitrarily detailed WITHOUT BLOATING THE EXECUTOR'S WORKING MEMORY.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: CONDITION on portability from the skill itself: 'This skill is project-agnostic. It works for any codebase that has a docs/goals/ (or equivalent) directory, CONVENTIONAL COMMITS, and some form of AS-BUILT / architecture doc.' Project toolchain commands are substituted wherever the templates say <project's ... command>.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's fill-in GOAL skeleton: a 'GOAL: <one-sentence headline>. <one paragraph: current pain -> what the goal lands -> headline word>' opener; **Read first.** as a bullet list of absolute paths (architecture doc, the rider being written, exemplars, prior riders); **Posture.** as one line of negations; a domain body; **Phases.** Eleven (P1-P11) in the rider; **Verification.** bullets of verifiable commands plus the no-edits-outside / no-push / no-schema-changes line; and **Stop when** verification passes, AS-BUILT updated, CHANGELOG has a milestone section, committed locally.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: TRIM PRIORITY when the goal is over the 4,000-char budget, in order: (1) drop parenthetical detail already in the rider; (2) shorten Read-first descriptions to bare absolute paths; (3) compress Posture to one or two lines; (4) cut verification smoke bullets to two; (5) drop cross-rider 'do not preempt' notes, which live in the rider. A stated gotcha: the -HHMM- insert costs ~5 chars per internal rider reference, so leave a buffer when riders cross-cite.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's RIDER skeleton opens with a title line, the goal's absolute path, an explicit 'It supersedes nothing in prior riders (<list dated rider filenames>) — their invariants still apply' clause, a one-line summary of what's new, and 'All paths absolute.' Its Posture section is headed 'Posture (decided — do not redesign)' and its Data model section is headed 'Data model (files, not fields)'. The Algorithms section carries pseudocode with the instruction 'The rider IS the spec — match it in the implementation.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The NO-V1-INVENTION clause, written into every rider's Posture: 'No V1 / next-tier invention. If a phase reveals a major architectural decision, log it in <V1-CANDIDATES path> and continue.' Restated as an engineering invariant: 'No silent expansion. Anything beyond P1-P11 goes into V1-CANDIDATES.md.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: A named engineering invariant that makes tests-first auditable after the fact: 'One depth test before each phase implementation. A PHASE WHOSE TESTS WERE NEVER RED IS SUSPECT.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: SPEC-PINNING INVARIANTS make formatting itself part of the contract — e.g. 'the preview block format is depth-tested; changing whitespace changes the spec.' The same move as the failure_reason regex: an agent cannot quietly relax what a test enumerates.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The rider's PROCESS INVARIANTS: phased local commits only, no git push; each phase ends with its depth tests passing and a CHANGELOG entry naming the SHA; after P11 optionally capture a demo (asciinema/screenshots/video), skipped when the change isn't user-visible; and if a phase reveals a V1-architecture decision, stop and log it in V1-CANDIDATES.md rather than silently expanding scope.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The rider's DEPENDENCIES section uses a three-tier policy: Tier 1 (utility, free) listed with a one-line justification each; Tier 2 (architectural) logged to DEPENDENCIES.md; Tier 3 (blocked) carrying the same blocks as prior riders.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's eleven-item DISCIPLINE CHECKLIST: two documents / two budgets (wc -c the goal); timestamped filenames sharing one minute; phased local commits only, never git push; files-not-fields; depth tests first, listed by name so grep enforces presence; architecture-doc discipline at P11 with an honest thin list; V1 candidates for anything out of scope; conventional commits scoped (docs(goals): for the pair itself); frontmatter mirroring the project's own convention; friendliness verifiable by depth test; and 'judgment in markdown, invariants in code' — prefer a skill/prompt-template mechanism over a hardcoded const.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The skill's ANTI-PATTERNS list: inventing V1 architecture inside an alpha rider; schema changes without a stated strong reason; backwards-compatibility shims no caller uses; comments explaining WHAT the code does; half-finished implementations ('we'll finish in P12'); duplicating prior riders' invariants verbatim instead of referencing them; depth tests written AFTER implementation; stop conditions that don't tie to verification ('stop when it feels done' is not a stop condition); inventing CLI verbs not in the goal; adding emojis to written artifacts; and 'TODO: maybe add X' lines — either it's P-numbered in scope or it's a V1 candidate.
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The single most transferable anti-pattern for authoring a completion condition: 'Stop conditions that don't tie to verification — "stop when it feels done" is NOT A STOP CONDITION.'
nodes.author: Greg Ceccarelli

nodes.label: The STANDARD 11-PHASE SHAPE (adapt names; eleven is a target, not a hard rule): P1 data model / plumbing with no behavior change yet; P2-P3 foundation (new primitive types, base mechanism); P4-P8 feature implementation, one phase per major slice each shipping end-to-end depth tests; P9 integration with prior verbs / modes / state machines; P10 a cross-cutting friendliness pass (--quiet / --plain flags, error-footer routing, post-action hints, help-text grouping); P11 architecture-doc update + CHANGELOG + optional demo capture, doc-only with no depth test.

nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: VERIFICATION field of the 5-part /goal template, glossed verbatim as 'the checker. How Claude proves it achieved your desired OUTCOME, not just lying to your face.'
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: Sabrina Ramonov names the bottleneck of /goal prompting outright: 'Hardest part is defining a clear measurable VERIFICATION step.'
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: Style rule for writing the two middle fields of a /goal: 'Be specific in OUTCOME and blunt in CONSTRAINTS.'
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: The article's sharpest good-vs-bad pair for a completion condition: '"Make it good" isn't a finish line. "Scores over 8+ out of 10 using my custom grading skill" is.' — the difference being a named instrument plus a numeric threshold.
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: The recap's load-bearing claim about what makes a /goal different from a prompt: 'VERIFICATION is what turns a prompt into an actual /goal that AI can use to introspect and drive towards completion.'
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: Both failure directions of a missing or weak VERIFICATION are named together: 'Without it, Claude has no way to prove OUTCOME actually happened, so it either stops too early or loops forever guessing.' — premature victory and non-termination are two faces of one defect.
nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: The article's operational test for a good completion condition: 'A good VERIFICATION line gives Claude something it can literally check, like a video, a click-through rate, or an open-hours confirmation.'

nodes.author: Sabrina Ramonov

nodes.label: Second exemplar of 'something it can literally check': a click-through rate — a measured metric that can be compared against a stated target.
