nodes.label: Anthropic's official Claude Code documentation page "Keep Claude working toward a goal" (code.claude.com/docs/en/goal.md) specifies the `/goal` command: how to set a completion condition, how the evaluator judges it after every turn, how to bound, clear, resume, and run it non-interactively, and when the command is unavailable.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT on any /goal condition: the evaluator "does not call tools, so it can only judge what Claude has already surfaced in the conversation." It runs no commands and reads no files independently, so any state the condition names must have been printed into the transcript by Claude itself before it can be judged true.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The authoring rule that follows directly from the evaluator having no tools: "write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate." A condition naming a fact only the filesystem or a process knows is unjudgeable unless the condition also compels Claude to surface that fact in the conversation.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The docs' worked example of a transcript-demonstrable condition: "All tests in `test/auth` pass" works because Claude runs the tests and the result lands in the transcript for the evaluator to read. The condition is judgeable not because it is precise but because running it produces evidence in the conversation.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Anthropic's template for a /goal condition that holds up across many turns: it usually has three parts — one measurable end state, a stated check, and constraints that matter. These three bullets are the docs' own structure for an effective condition, not a community convention.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Part 1 of an effective /goal condition — ONE MEASURABLE END STATE: "a test result, a build exit code, a file count, an empty queue." The end state must be a single countable or pass/fail fact, not a quality aspiration.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Part 2 of an effective /goal condition — A STATED CHECK, meaning "how Claude should prove it, such as \"`npm test` exits 0\" or \"`git status` is clean\"." The condition names the proof procedure, not only the desired state: it says which command Claude runs and what result counts as passing.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Part 3 of an effective /goal condition — CONSTRAINTS THAT MATTER: "anything that must not change on the way there, such as \"no other test file is modified\"." These are the negative clauses that keep the agent from reaching the end state by an illegitimate route.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A /goal condition can be up to 4,000 characters. That is the hard authoring budget for the whole condition text, which is re-sent to the evaluator alongside the conversation on every turn.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: One goal can be active per session, and the same `/goal` command sets, checks, and clears it depending on the argument given. There is no multi-goal mode.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Setting a goal is `/goal` followed by the condition you want satisfied; if a goal is already active, the new one silently REPLACES it rather than erroring or stacking.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Setting a goal STARTS A TURN IMMEDIATELY, with the condition itself as the directive — no separate prompt is needed. Consequence for authoring: the condition text is simultaneously a predicate the evaluator judges and the first instruction the working model receives, so it must read as a workable directive.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: While a goal is active, Claude Code displays a `◎ /goal active` indicator showing how long the goal has been running.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The docs' canonical interactive example of setting a goal: `/goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean` — a conjunction of two transcript-demonstrable checks.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Goals are for substantial work with a verifiable end state. The docs' four examples: migrating a module to a new API until every call site compiles and tests pass; implementing a design doc until all acceptance criteria hold; splitting a large file into focused modules until each is under a size budget; working through a labeled issue backlog until the queue is empty.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The /goal loop in one sentence: after each turn a small fast model checks whether the condition holds; if it does not, Claude starts another turn instead of returning control to the user, and the goal clears automatically once the condition is met.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` requires Claude Code v2.1.139 or later; on earlier versions the command does not exist.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: MECHANISM: `/goal` is a wrapper around a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook. It is not a separate subsystem — everything the Stop-hook and prompt-hook contracts say about wire behaviour applies to it.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Each time Claude finishes a turn, the condition AND the conversation so far are sent to the session's configured small fast model. That model defaults to Haiku on the Claude API only — a third-party provider substitutes its own, and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL replaces it outright. The evaluator therefore reads the whole transcript, so evidence in a long run competes for attention with everything else in it. (Re-verified 2026-07-30; 'defaults to Haiku' was unqualified until then.)
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The evaluator model returns a yes-or-no decision plus a short reason. A "no" tells Claude to keep working and includes the reason as guidance for the next turn; a "yes" clears the goal and records an achieved entry in the transcript.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The /goal evaluator runs on whichever provider the session is configured for — it is not pinned to Anthropic's own API when the session points elsewhere.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Evaluation tokens are billed on the small fast model configured for the provider and are "typically negligible compared to main-turn spend" — the per-turn evaluator is not a meaningful cost driver of a goal run.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: After each turn the evaluator returns a short reason explaining why the condition is or is not met, and the most recent reason appears both in the `/goal` status view and in the transcript, so a human can see what Claude is working toward next.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The hooks reference confirms the same mechanism from the other side: "The `/goal` command is a built-in shortcut for a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook. Use it when you want Claude to keep working until a condition holds without writing hook configuration."
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: How a prompt-based hook (the machinery behind /goal) works: (1) the hook input and the prompt are sent to a Claude model, Haiku by default; (2) the LLM responds with structured JSON containing a decision; (3) Claude Code processes the decision automatically. No Bash command is executed.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The exact JSON a prompt-hook evaluator must emit is `{"ok": true | false, "reason": "Explanation for the decision"}`. `ok: true` allows; `ok: false` produces a `decision: "block"`, and `reason` is REQUIRED when `ok` is false because it is used as the block reason.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: On `ok: false` for the `Stop` and `SubagentStop` events, "the reason is fed back to Claude as its next instruction and the turn continues." The evaluator's rejection text therefore literally becomes the working model's prompt — a badly worded reason steers the next turn badly.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A prompt-type hook has a default `timeout` of 30 seconds (versus 600 for command/http/mcp_tool hooks). The docs do not state what /goal does when its evaluator times out.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Prompt hooks accept a `continueOnBlock` field (default `false`): when the prompt returns `ok: false`, feed the reason back to Claude and continue the turn instead of stopping. It is implemented as `continue: true` on the resulting `decision: "block"`. For `Stop` the reason is fed back regardless, so this field is the knob that could make /goal's continuation behaviour differ from a plain Stop hook's.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A prompt hook accepts an optional `model` field selecting the model used for evaluation, defaulting to a fast model — which is why /goal's evaluator is described as "your configured small fast model, which defaults to Haiku" rather than as a fixed model.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The `Stop` event — the event /goal is built on — "runs when the main Claude Code agent has finished responding." It does NOT run if the stoppage occurred due to a user interrupt.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: When a turn ends due to an API error, `StopFailure` fires INSTEAD of `Stop`, and StopFailure hooks have no decision control (output and exit code are ignored). A goal turn killed by a rate limit or auth error is therefore not evaluated by the goal evaluator at all.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Stop hooks receive a `stop_hook_active` input field that is `true` when Claude Code is already continuing as a result of a stop hook. The docs tell hook authors to check it "to avoid blocking on a condition that will never resolve" — the built-in signal that an unsatisfiable condition is the expected failure mode of this design.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A Stop hook's decision-control fields: `decision: "block"` prevents Claude from stopping (omit it to allow the stop), `reason` is required with a block and tells Claude why it should continue, and `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` supplies non-error feedback that also continues the conversation but is labelled "Stop hook feedback" instead of a hook error.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `additionalContext` on a Stop hook "keeps the conversation going through the same loop protections as `decision: \"block\"`, namely the `stop_hook_active` input and the 8-consecutive-continuation cap" — confirming the cap is a property of the Stop continuation machinery generally, not of one output shape.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: To bound how long a goal runs, the ONLY documented mechanism is to include a turn or time clause inside the condition text itself, such as `or stop after 20 turns`. Nothing outside the condition bounds a goal run.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A turn/time bound in a /goal condition is NOT harness-enforced: "Claude reports progress against that clause each turn and the evaluator judges it from the conversation." The bound is a self-report read out of the transcript, with the same no-tools limitation as every other clause.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: goal.md's stopping claim: "A goal keeps running until the condition is met or you run `/goal clear`." The page states no turn cap, no iteration limit, and no automatic override anywhere in its text.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: hooks.md's opposing claim about the same machinery: "Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks." Stated as a property of Stop hooks generally, which is what /goal is implemented as.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: UNRECONCILED DOC DISAGREEMENT: hooks.md says Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after 8 consecutive blocks, while goal.md says a goal keeps running until the condition is met or cleared and never mentions any cap. /goal IS a prompt-based Stop hook, which argues the cap applies; goal.md's unbounded language and the `continueOnBlock` field argue the wrapper may set it differently. Neither page reconciles the other — do not design a condition assuming either statement governs.
`/goal clear` removes an active goal before its condition is met. Claude prints `Goal cleared:` followed by the condition to confirm, or `No goal set` if nothing was active.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `stop`, `off`, `reset`, `none`, and `cancel` are all accepted as aliases for `clear` — `/goal stop` and `/goal cancel` do exactly what `/goal clear` does.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Running `/clear` to start a new conversation ALSO removes any active goal. The documented fix for a context polluted by failed approaches therefore destroys the goal at the same time.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Running `/goal` with no arguments shows the current state rather than setting anything — it is the status verb of the same command.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: When a goal is active, `/goal` status shows five things: the condition, how long it has been running, how many turns have been evaluated, the current token spend, and the evaluator's most recent reason.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: In the `/goal` status view, the turn count and the most recent reason only appear AFTER the first evaluation has run — their absence right after setting a goal is expected, not a fault.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: If no goal is active but one was achieved earlier in the session, `/goal` status shows the achieved condition along with its duration, turn count, and token spend — a completed run stays inspectable for the rest of the session.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A goal still active when a session ended IS restored when that session is resumed with `--resume` or `--continue`; the condition carries over intact.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: On resume, the turn count, the timer, and the token-spend baseline ALL RESET even though the condition carries over. A `or stop after 20 turns` clause therefore silently re-arms on every resume: a turn or time bound is not a durable budget across sessions.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A goal that was already achieved or cleared is NOT restored on resume — only a goal that was still active when the session ended comes back.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` runs only in workspaces where the trust dialog has been accepted, because the evaluator is part of the hooks system. An untrusted workspace has no /goal.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` is unavailable when `disableAllHooks` is set at ANY settings level — because /goal is a hook, disabling hooks anywhere in the settings chain removes the command.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` is also unavailable when `allowManagedHooksOnly` is set in MANAGED settings — an enterprise policy that permits only managed hooks blocks the session-scoped hook /goal installs.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: In every unavailability case — untrusted workspace, `disableAllHooks`, `allowManagedHooksOnly` — "the command tells you why instead of silently doing nothing." A /goal that appears to do nothing is not the documented failure shape.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: A goal does NOT change permissions. In the default permission mode Claude still asks before tool calls that the settings don't already allow — including the very test command named in the condition — so an unattended goal run can stall on a permission prompt every turn.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: To let goal turns run unattended, the docs' explicit instruction is to pair `/goal` with auto mode. Without it, permission prompts, not the condition, decide how far an unattended run gets.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Auto mode and /goal are complementary and orthogonal: auto mode approves tool calls WITHIN a single turn but doesn't start a new one, while /goal starts new turns but doesn't approve tools. "Auto mode removes per-tool prompts, and `/goal` removes per-turn prompts."
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The design intent of /goal: it adds a separate evaluator that checks the condition after every turn, "so completion is decided by a fresh model rather than the one doing the work." Without it, Claude stops when it judges the work done — the worker grades itself.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Three approaches keep the current session running between prompts — `/goal`, `/loop`, and a Stop hook — and the docs say to pick based on WHAT SHOULD START THE NEXT TURN, not on what the work is.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Comparison row for `/goal`: the next turn starts when the previous turn finishes, and it stops when A MODEL CONFIRMS THE CONDITION IS MET.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Comparison row for `/loop`: the next turn starts when A TIME INTERVAL ELAPSES, and it stops when you stop it or Claude decides the work is done — i.e. /loop has no independent completion judge, unlike /goal.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Comparison row for a Stop hook: the next turn starts when the previous turn finishes (same trigger as /goal), and it stops when YOUR OWN SCRIPT OR PROMPT DECIDES — the deterministic-check option.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` and a Stop hook both fire after every turn; the difference is scope and authoring. /goal is a session-scoped shortcut you type as a condition and it is active for the current session only, while a Stop hook lives in a settings file, applies to every session in its scope, and can run a SCRIPT for deterministic checks or a prompt for model-evaluated ones.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: All three session-keeping approaches keep the CURRENT session running; work that must run independent of any open session (nightly tests, morning triage) belongs to the separate scheduling options — cloud routines and desktop scheduled tasks — not to /goal.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: `/goal` works in non-interactive (headless) mode, in the desktop app, and through Remote Control — it is not an interactive-TUI-only feature.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Setting a goal with `-p` runs the whole loop to completion in a SINGLE invocation, e.g. `claude -p "/goal CHANGELOG.md has an entry for every PR merged this week"` — the process does not return until the condition is met or it is interrupted.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: With the default text output in headless mode, NOTHING PRINTS until the condition is met, so a goal that runs many turns can look stuck. Add `--output-format stream-json --verbose` to emit each message as the loop runs.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Interrupt the process with Ctrl+C to stop a non-interactive goal before its condition is met — the headless equivalent of `/goal clear`.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Slash-stacking: several skills can be stacked at the start of one message (`/write-tests /fix-issue 123` loads both and passes the trailing text as `$ARGUMENTS` to each). Claude Code expands the first skill plus up to five more stacked after it.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: Slash-command expansion STOPS at the first token that isn't an inline user-invocable skill — so a skill that runs as a FORKED SUBAGENT (such as `/code-review`), or one whose arguments may themselves start with a slash command (such as `/loop`), ends the expansion run there. That token and everything after it become the argument text for every already-expanded skill.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: best-practices.md places /goal on a ladder of how hard a check gates the stop: in one prompt (ask Claude to run the check and iterate), across a session (a `/goal` condition re-checked by a separate evaluator after every turn), as a deterministic gate (a Stop hook script — "Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks"), or by a second opinion (a verification subagent). This is the third page repeating the 8-block cap for Stop hooks.
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: The Claude Code glossary states a verification loop — a check Claude can run and iterate against — is the PREREQUISITE for `/goal`, unattended runs, and dynamic workflows: "without one, the only thing deciding the agent is finished is the agent itself."
nodes.author: Anthropic

nodes.label: GAP: no Claude Code doc describes a way for a /goal condition to declare "I am blocked, hand control back to the human" as a first-class outcome. The only documented exits are: the evaluator returns yes; `/goal clear` or an alias; `/clear`; Ctrl+C in headless mode; and — for Stop hooks generally, disputed for /goal — the 8-consecutive-block override.
